Gross Pay vs Net Pay: What Each Number on Your Pay Stub Really Means

Direct AnswerGross pay vs net pay explained: the definitions, every deduction between them — federal tax, FICA, state tax, 401(k), premiums — plus worked examples.

Gross pay estimates
By Saahil•Published October 23, 2026•10 min read•Tax & Payroll Guides
A closer look

In this guide

The Short AnswerWhat Gross Pay MeansWhat Net Pay (Take-Home) MeansThe Deductions Between ThemExample: A $60,000 Salary, Step by StepExample: $25 an Hour, Full-TimeHow to Read Your Pay StubGross vs Net in Real DecisionsFrequently Asked QuestionsKey Takeaways & Action Plan

Use your actual work schedule for a more useful estimate.

Every pay stub tells two stories about the same work. At the top sits your gross pay — the full amount you earned. At the bottom sits your net pay — what actually lands in your bank account. On a $60,000 salary, that gap is roughly $9,610 a year in federal tax and FICA alone, before state tax or a single benefit deduction. This guide explains both numbers, everything that is taken out between them, and how to run the calculation yourself.

Confusing the two figures leads to predictable mistakes: budgeting on the gross amount named in an offer letter, comparing job offers by salary alone, or assuming a first paycheck contains an error when the math is in fact correct. The sections below trace every step from gross to net, so that each line on your stub has a clear explanation.

The Short Answer

Gross pay is your total earnings before deductions. Net pay is gross pay minus every deduction — taxes, retirement contributions, insurance premiums and any other withholding. The formula is one line:

Net Pay = Gross Pay − All Deductions

The rest of this guide breaks down what sits inside "all deductions" — and how large each piece typically is.

Gross PayNet Pay
MeaningEverything you earnedEverything you keep
IncludesWages, salary, overtime, bonuses, commissions, tipsWhat remains after taxes and deductions
Used forJob offers, contracts, loan applications, tax returnsBudgeting, bill paying, saving goals
On your stubTop line, before deductionsBottom line — matches your deposit

What Gross Pay Means

Gross pay is the full value of your compensation for a pay period, before anything is withheld. For hourly workers it is your hours multiplied by your rate, including the overtime premium for hours past 40 in a week. For salaried workers it is the annual salary divided across your pay periods. Either way, it counts all of these when they occur:

  • Base wages or salary for the period
  • Overtime pay, shift differentials and holiday premiums
  • Bonuses and commissions
  • Reported tips
  • Paid time off taken during the period

The two formulas that produce gross pay:

Hourly: Gross = (Hours × Rate) + (Overtime Hours × Rate × 0.5)
Salaried: Gross per check = Annual Salary ÷ Pay Periods per Year

A $60,000 salary paid biweekly (26 checks) is $2,307.69 of gross pay per check. To convert any rate or salary yourself, use the hourly to salary calculator.

Gross pay is the number the outside world runs on. Employers advertise it, contracts state it, lenders ask for it, and your tax return starts from it. It is a real number — it is just not the number that pays your rent.

What Net Pay (Take-Home) Means

Net pay is the amount your employer actually hands over after withholding everything the law requires and everything you signed up for. If you have direct deposit, your net pay is the deposit — to the cent. If your deposit ever differs from the net pay line on your stub, that is a genuine error worth raising with payroll the same day.

Why is gross pay always the quoted figure? Because net pay is personal. Two coworkers with identical salaries can have different net pay because one files taxes as single and the other as married, one contributes 10% to a 401(k) and the other nothing, one covers a family health plan and the other is on a spouse's. No employer can quote a net figure honestly, so the entire labor market quotes gross — and translating it into take-home pay is what the rest of this guide does.

The Deductions Between Them

Between the top line and the bottom line of your stub sit three groups of deductions, almost always in this order:

GroupDeductionsCan you change it?
Required taxesFederal income tax · Social Security 6.2% (wages up to $184,500 in 2026) · Medicare 1.45% · State and local income taxOnly at the margins — your W-4 adjusts federal withholding
Your choices401(k)/403(b) contributions · Health, dental and vision premiums · HSA/FSA deposits · Union duesYes — at enrollment, open enrollment, or any time for retirement contributions
Court-ordered & otherWage garnishments · Child support · Tax levies · Post-tax items like Roth contributionsOnly through the court or agency that ordered it

Two details explain most stub surprises. First, order matters for taxes: pre-tax deductions come out before income tax is calculated, so a 401(k) contribution lowers your federal (and usually state) tax bill — but it does not lower FICA, which is charged on nearly your full gross. Health premiums paid through a workplace plan usually reduce both income-tax wages and FICA wages. Second, FICA has two different rules inside it: Social Security stops at $184,500 of 2026 wages, while Medicare's 1.45% never stops — and a further 0.9% Medicare tax applies once wages pass $200,000. For the full tax-by-tax walk-through, see our guide to how taxes are calculated on a paycheck.

Example: A $60,000 Salary, Step by Step

The baseline example uses a single filer earning $60,000 in 2026, claiming the standard deduction of $16,100, with no benefit deductions — taxes only. Federal income tax first: taxable income is $60,000 − $16,100 = $43,900, which fills the 10% bracket ($12,400 × 10% = $1,240) and part of the 12% bracket ($31,500 × 12% = $3,780), for $5,020 total. FICA is simpler: 7.65% of the full $60,000 = $4,590.

LinePer Year
Gross pay$60,000
Federal income tax−$5,020
Social Security (6.2%)−$3,720
Medicare (1.45%)−$870
Net pay (no state income tax)$50,390 — 84.0% of gross
State income tax (5% example)−$3,000
Net pay (with 5% state tax)$47,390 — 79.0% of gross

In paycheck terms (biweekly): gross of $2,307.69 becomes $1,938.08 deposited — or $1,822.69 in the 5%-state version. Monthly take-home is $4,199.17 with no state tax. That monthly figure, not $5,000, is the honest starting point for a budget.

Example: $25 an Hour, Full-Time

Now an hourly worker: $25 an hour, 40 hours a week, 52 weeks — a gross of $52,000. Same single filer, same 2026 standard deduction:

LinePer Year
Gross pay$52,000
Federal income tax (on $35,900 taxable)−$4,060
FICA (7.65%)−$3,978
Net pay (no state income tax)$43,962 — 84.5% of gross

Per biweekly check: $2,000.00 gross becomes $1,690.85 net; monthly take-home averages $3,663.50. Notice the slightly better percentage than the $60,000 earner — a smaller share of this income reaches the 12% bracket's upper end, so the effective tax bite is lighter.

The same worker, with voluntary deductions. Give this worker a 5% 401(k) contribution ($2,600) and a $150-a-month health premium ($1,800). Federal tax falls to $3,532 — both deductions come out before income tax — and FICA falls slightly to $3,840.30, because the premium (unlike the 401(k)) also escapes FICA. The new net: $40,227.70 a year, 77.4% of gross, or $1,547.22 a check. The deposit dropped by about $144 a check — but $100 of it went into the worker's own retirement account, which is why a smaller net is not always a worse outcome.

How to Read Your Pay Stub

Your stub is the source of truth for both numbers. Almost every stub shows two columns: Current (this pay period) and YTD (year to date). The gross pay in the YTD column is the figure that should track toward your annual salary; the current column is what this check's net was built from. Common abbreviations, translated:

Stub LabelMeans
FIT / Fed TaxFederal income tax withheld
SS / OASDI / FICA-SSSocial Security tax (6.2%)
MED / FICA-MEDMedicare tax (1.45%)
SIT / State TaxState income tax withheld
401k / RETYour retirement contribution
NET PAYYour deposit — gross minus everything above it

A useful monthly habit: check that YTD gross divided by checks received matches your expected per-check gross. It catches rate errors early — and it explains why some months feel richer: in a three-paycheck month, your monthly net jumps even though neither your gross rate nor your deductions changed.

Gross vs Net in Real Decisions

Comparing job offers: compare gross pay and benefits together — gross is the common yardstick — but before accepting, translate the winner into net. An offer with cheaper health premiums can beat a slightly higher salary once both are run to the bottom line.

Budgeting: budget only on net. Rent, the 50/30/20 split, savings goals — all of them must be built from deposits, not offer letters. Our $23 an hour guide shows the method: its whole monthly budget is built from the take-home figure, not the $47,840 gross.

Negotiating a raise: raises are quoted gross, received net. A $2-an-hour raise is $4,160 a year of gross — and at the keep-rates in this guide, roughly $3,300 a year of actual deposits, about $127 more per biweekly check. Knowing that conversion keeps both your expectations and your counter-offer honest.

Loans and taxes: lenders qualify you on gross income, because it is standardized and verifiable; your tax return starts from gross wages and works down through its own deductions. Net pay is for your household math — gross is for everyone else's paperwork.

Frequently Asked Questions

Quick answers to the questions readers ask most about gross and net pay.

What is the difference between gross pay and net pay?

Gross pay is everything you earn before anything is taken out — wages, overtime, bonuses and commissions at their full value. Net pay is what remains after every deduction: federal and state taxes, Social Security and Medicare (FICA), retirement contributions, health insurance premiums and anything else on your stub. Net pay is the amount that actually reaches your bank account, which is why it is also called take-home pay.

How do I calculate net pay from gross pay?

Work through your stub in order: start with gross pay for the period, subtract pre-tax items (401(k) contributions and health premiums), calculate federal income tax on what remains after the standard deduction, subtract FICA — 7.65% for most workers — then state and local tax, and finally any post-tax deductions such as Roth contributions or garnishments. What is left is your net pay. Our paycheck calculator runs this same sequence for your own numbers.

What gets deducted from gross pay?

Three groups. Required taxes: federal income tax, Social Security (6.2% on wages up to $184,500 in 2026), Medicare (1.45% on all wages), and state or local income tax where it applies. Voluntary deductions you chose: 401(k) or 403(b) contributions, health, dental and vision premiums, HSA or FSA deposits, and union dues. And court-ordered or other withholdings: wage garnishments, child support and tax levies. Not every stub has all three groups, but the order on the stub almost always follows them.

Is your salary quoted as gross or net?

Always gross. Job offers, salary bands, raise letters and hourly rates are all stated before deductions, because your employer cannot know your personal tax situation — your filing status, second job, or benefit choices change the net. That is why a first paycheck often looks surprisingly small next to the offer: a $60,000 salary does not deposit $5,000 a month; it deposits roughly $4,199 a month in take-home pay in a state with no income tax, and less where state tax applies.

What percentage of your paycheck is take-home pay?

There is no single percentage, but the worked examples in this guide land between 79% and 84.5% of gross after taxes alone — a $60,000 salary keeps 84.0% in a state with no income tax and 79.0% with a 5% state tax. Add voluntary deductions like a 401(k) contribution and health premiums and the deposited share typically falls into the 70% to 80% range. Higher incomes keep a smaller share because more of their pay is taxed in higher brackets.

What does “gross up” mean?

Grossing up is when an employer pays extra so that you receive a specific net amount after tax. Instead of handing you a $500 bonus that shrinks to about $352 after 22% federal withholding and 7.65% FICA, the employer pays $710.73 — calculated as $500 ÷ (1 − 0.2965) — so that after those same deductions you keep exactly $500. Gross-ups are common for relocation bonuses, awards and executive perks.

Key Takeaways & Action Plan

What to Remember

  • Net = gross − all deductions. Offers and salaries are always gross; your deposit is always net.
  • Taxes are the biggest wedge: on a $60,000 salary, federal tax plus FICA take $9,610 — keeping 84.0% before state tax, 79.0% with a 5% state tax.
  • Pre-tax is not all equal: a 401(k) skips income tax but not FICA; workplace health premiums usually skip both.
  • Your stub is the source of truth: net pay should match your deposit to the cent, and YTD gross should track your salary.
  • Budget on net, compare on gross — and translate every offer to take-home before you sign.

How We Calculated These Examples

Examples use 2026 federal figures (IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32): a $16,100 standard deduction for single filers, the 10% bracket to $12,400 of taxable income and 12% to $50,400, plus FICA at 6.2% Social Security (2026 wage base $184,500) and 1.45% Medicare. Both example workers are single filers paid biweekly with no credits or additional adjustments; the state variant uses a flat 5% for illustration. Your withholding during the year is an estimate settled on your tax return, so your own stub will differ — the order and method will not.
